notes: VAT face-value voucher judicial review; Sixth Directive place-of-supply analysis and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: IDT Card Services: VAT on Irish multifunctional phonecards under Schedule 10A
key_facts: IDT Card Services Ireland supplied multifunctional phonecards from Ireland to UK distributors; redemption gave access to Irish telecommunications services via Interdirect.
Irish VAT law treats card sales as prepayment for telecoms, while UK law taxes the telecom service on redemption; the structure risked double non-taxation.
HMRC argued Schedule 10A paragraph 3 required VAT on card supplies to UK traders via reverse charge, or that ICSIL and Interdirect were the same person so paragraph 4 applied.
The business plan predated Schedule 10A and Moses J found no abusive tax avoidance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging HMRC assessments on supplies of prepaid phonecards and related telecommunications services.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the United Kingdom had no Sixth Directive basis to charge VAT on Interdirect's Irish telecom supplies to UK end-users outside Article 9(2)(e), and paragraph 3(3) could not be construed to treat Interdirect as having failed to account for EU VAT.
enrichment.ratio: Article 9 allocates VAT jurisdiction between Member States and does not empower one state to tax a supply whose place of supply under Article 9(1) lies in another Member State merely to avoid non-taxation; domestic Schedule 10A must be read consistently with that territorial scheme.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 3(3) 'VAT due' includes VAT due anywhere in the European Union
Whether ICSIL and Interdirect were the same person for paragraph 3(1) purposes
Whether Marleasing construction could require UK taxation to prevent non-taxation
Whether the structures amounted to abusive tax avoidance
linked_authorities: Argos Distribution Ltd v Customs and Excise [1997] QB 499
Gemeente Leusden v Staatsecretaris van Financien (C-487/01)
Jurgen Dudda v Finanzamt Bergisch Gladbach (C-327/94)

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and final disposition are clearly reasoned; leave to appeal was granted.

notes: Section 28(1)(a) 'immediately' construction; appeal allowed and aggravated conviction quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Parry v DPP: 'immediately' in racially aggravated criminal damage
key_facts: Peter Parry threw nail varnish over his neighbour Mrs McCleery's front door shortly before midnight on 24 January 2004.
About twenty minutes later, when police questioned him at home, he used abusive language referring to 'Irish cunts' and 'IRA bastards'.
He admitted criminal damage but denied the offence was racially aggravated under section 28(1)(a).
The Crown Court upheld conviction; Field LJ held the hostile words were not made immediately after the substantive offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Chester Crown Court dismissing an appeal against conviction for racially aggravated criminal damage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Crown Court decision and the magistrates' conviction on the aggravated charge were quashed; questions 1 answered yes and question 6 answered no.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 28(1)(a) 'immediately' qualifies both 'before' and 'after' the substantive offence and requires demonstration of hostility in the immediate context of that offence; hostility may be shown towards an absent victim but not after the offender has quit the scene.
legal_issues: Whether 'immediately' in section 28(1)(a) applies to hostility demonstrated after the offence
Whether a twenty-minute gap after the damage precluded an 'immediately after' finding
Whether hostility to a police officer in the defendant's home could be hostility towards the victim
Whether the victim must be present when hostility is demonstrated

confidence.notes: Agreed facts and narrow statutory construction point are clearly resolved.

notes: Securicor conspiracy appeal; PTSD fresh evidence admitted and both convictions unsafe.

enrichment.short_title: R v Huckerby and Power: PTSD evidence and £6.5m Securicor robbery conspiracy
key_facts: On 3 July 1995 over £6.5 million was stolen from a Securicor van at a Midland Bank sorting office in Salford; Huckerby was the inside driver and Power was alleged to be his handler.
The Crown case rested on circumstantial inference from Huckerby's failure to activate tracking devices, telephone contact, cash deposits and a disputed confession to Clare Healey.
Fresh psychiatric evidence suggested Huckerby suffered PTSD from an earlier 1994 robbery affecting his conduct during the 1995 attack.
Both appellants were convicted on retrial after other co-accused were acquitted or had indictments stayed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for leave to adduce fresh psychiatric evidence and appeals against conviction and confiscation orders following a second trial.
enrichment.outcome: Fresh evidence of Dr Green and Mr Regel admitted; both convictions held unsafe and appeals allowed; confiscation orders set aside; retrial to be considered.
enrichment.ratio: Expert evidence on recognised PTSD may be admissible where the prosecution case depends on inferring willing participation from the defendant's conduct, even absent a formal duress plea; on appeal such evidence may be admitted under section 23 where trial counsel could not have deployed it and overall safety is in doubt.
legal_issues: Whether psychiatric evidence supporting the defendant's account was inadmissible oath-helping
Whether fresh PTSD evidence should be admitted years after trial under section 23
Whether telephone call evidence to third-party addresses remained probative after co-accused were acquitted
Whether the judge's summing-up on telephone evidence was adequate
linked_authorities: R v Robinson [1994] 98 Crim App R (S) 370
R v Bowen [1996] 2 Cr App R (S) 157

confidence.notes: Detailed reserved judgment on fresh evidence and telephone evidence; retrial not finally determined.

notes: PFI M&E subcontract preliminary issues; Court of Appeal upheld £14m cap not £34.25m obligation.

enrichment.short_title: Emcor v McAlpine: scope of Dudley Hospitals PFI mechanical and electrical subcontract
key_facts: Sir Robert McAlpine was main contractor on the Dudley Hospitals PFI project with about £34.25 million of M&E works.
Emcor began work under a 3 July 2001 short-form purchase order capped at £1 million pending a formal DOM subcontract that was never executed.
A series of capped orders followed (£3m, £8m, £14m aggregate); McAlpine rejected a final £34.285m order in October 2002 and purported to accept repudiatory breach.
McAlpine relied on an 20 August 2001 side letter as binding Emcor to the full M&E package for £34.25 million.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issues trial determining whether Emcor was contractually bound to complete all M&E works for £34.25 million.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Emcor was obliged only to perform work up to the cumulative order caps (ultimately £14 million), not the entire M&E scope; costs appeal permission refused.
enrichment.ratio: Read together, the capped short-form orders and the 20 August letter contemplated future formal subcontract terms rather than a present agreement for the whole works; successive limited orders showed the parties never agreed Emcor would carry out all M&E work before execution of a conforming subcontract.
legal_issues: Whether the 20 August 2001 letter bound Emcor to complete all M&E works for £34.25 million
Whether work performed under capped purchase orders evidenced a whole-works contract
Whether unresolved liability mismatches between draft and main contract terms prevented binding agreement
Whether the judge erred in ordering McAlpine to pay preliminary issue costs

notes: Lloyd's Energy '77 Cover trial; Morison J rejected all reinsurer defences in general conclusion.

enrichment.short_title: Bonner v Cox: Lloyd's Energy '77 Cover reinsurance debt and avoidance defences
key_facts: Lloyd's energy syndicates 535, 62, 187 and 228 sued reinsurers Cox, Euclidian (1243), 1688 and broker AON for debts under the AON-operated Energy '77 Open Cover.
Reinsurers pleaded avoidance for non-disclosure of the Elk Point loss and misrepresentations about business type, writing against and long-term declarations.
The 1999 year cover reinsurance involved complex fronting and retrocession arrangements with Tryg Baltica and syndicate 1688.
Part of the multi-party litigation settled during trial; Morison J held none of the remaining defences had substance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of debt claims by Lloyd's syndicates with extensive reinsurer defences and cross-claims against brokers.
enrichment.outcome: All reinsurer defences rejected; coverage issues decided in claimants' favour on long-term declarations and non-standard security; parties directed to draw up the order giving effect to judgment.
enrichment.ratio: The 1999 reinsurance slip, read with the MOU and risks-attaching wording, covered long-term declarations re-signed into the 1999 year without temporal limit; annual re-signing does not cancel underlying cover, and alleged Elk Point non-disclosure did not justify avoidance on the facts found.
legal_issues: Whether undisclosed Elk Point loss information induced syndicates 1688 and 1243 to write cover reinsurance
Whether cover underwriters engaged in impermissible 'writing against' the reinsurance
Whether long-term declarations and non-standard security fell within reinsurance coverage
Whether AON breached duties or warranties to syndicates if avoidance defences succeeded
linked_authorities: Baker v Black Sea and Baltic General Insurance Co [1996] 1 Lloyd's Rep 353

notes: Secure tenancy anti-social behaviour appeal; judge erred on suspended possession reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Norwich CC v Famuyiwa: reasonableness of possession for tenant nuisance
key_facts: Miss Famuyiwa was a secure tenant at 26 Clifton Close, Norwich, with over ten years' previously unproblematic occupation.
From late 2001 neighbours complained of door slamming, abusive language and confrontational behaviour over about 78 alleged incidents.
The deputy judge found grounds 1 and 2 made out but refused possession as unreasonable, instead granting a two-year injunction.
Neighbours including Mr Bowhill gave credible evidence that the tenant's conduct made life miserable, especially affecting a young child.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Norwich County Court refusal to make a possession order in secure tenancy proceedings for nuisance and harassment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; possession order made with date postponed pending county court determination of section 85(3) terms; injunction left undisturbed; costs ordered against tenant.
enrichment.ratio: In deciding reasonableness under section 84(2)(a) the court must consider whether a postponed or suspended possession order under section 85 could control behaviour; it was wrong in principle to dismiss possession because a suspended order seemed pointless without examining appropriate conditions.
legal_issues: Whether it was reasonable to refuse possession despite established nuisance under ground 2
Whether the judge erred by conflating section 84(2)(a) and section 85(2)-(3) stages
Whether an injunction rather than a suspended possession order was appropriate
Whether long prior good tenancy history outweighed persistent breach
linked_authorities: West Kent Housing Association Ltd v Davies (1998) 31 HLR 415
Raeuchle v Laimond Properties Ltd (2001) 33 HLR 10
Canterbury City Council v Lowe (2001) 33 HLR 53

notes: Stolen Mercedes insurance fraud trial; appeal dismissed on fraud findings and CWS distinguished.

enrichment.short_title: Interface v Eagle Star: good faith and alleged theft of financed Mercedes
key_facts: Interface Properties claimed indemnity for the alleged theft of a Mercedes bought from Jalal Din, who was fraudulently selling a vehicle still subject to Benton Finance hire purchase.
Asad Chaudhary said he inspected the car on 6 May 2000 and completed purchase on 8 May, but Bensons' records showed the car remained in Leeds until 7 May.
Eagle Star denied any genuine transfer and put the claimant to proof of purchase and theft; the recorder found Chaudhary an unsatisfactory witness.
The recorder held the AA check on 6 May was made to support a false story and ordered indemnity costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Central London County Court dismissal of claim for indemnity and ownership declaration after trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; recorder entitled to find no good-faith acquisition or genuine theft; unfair motivation finding on AA call insufficient to vitiate overall decision.
enrichment.ratio: Where the insurer's case throughout amounted to allegations of fraud, a trial judge may find dishonesty on issues directly raised even if one specific motivation finding was not put; that isolated unfairness does not require retrial when other fraud findings amply support dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether the judge made unpleaded fraud findings in breach of audi alteram partem
Whether finding that the AA call supported a false story was unfairly made without cross-examination on that point
Whether Bensons' evidence proved the Mercedes could not have been seen in London on 6 May
Whether indemnity costs were appropriate
linked_authorities: Co-operative (CWS) Ltd v International Computers Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 1955
Vogon International Ltd v SFO [2004] EWCA Civ 104

notes: Orchard Hill closure directions; Coughlan and Wilkinson require merits review of best interests.

enrichment.short_title: CH v Sutton and Merton PCT: Orchard Hill Hospital closure and home-for-life promises
key_facts: Orchard Hill Hospital in Carshalton housed 102 adults with severe learning disabilities; the PCT decided on 20 May 2004 to close it.
Many residents had been given 'home for life' promises; a 2000 closure decision had been quashed by Jackson J for failing to assess individual needs.
Clinical assessment suggested most residents would suffer heightened or disabling emotional harm from relocation.
The PCT contended closure was in residents' best interests and justified overriding the promises under Coughlan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management directions in linked judicial review and Part 8 family proceedings challenging hospital closure.
enrichment.outcome: Court held disputed best-interests issues require full merits determination on oral evidence, not conventional judicial review alone; proceedings to be heard together and remitted for that enquiry.
enrichment.ratio: Where a public body relies on residents' best interests to override legitimate expectations from home-for-life promises, Coughlan and Wilkinson require the court itself to resolve disputed factual issues about those best interests rather than deferring to the decision-maker under Wednesbury review.
legal_issues: Whether closure decision lawfully overrode home-for-life promises
Whether adequate individual needs assessments were conducted
Whether the court must conduct a merits review of best interests under Article 8
How linked judicial review and family proceedings should be case-managed
linked_authorities: R v North and East Devon Health Authority ex p Coughlan [2001] QB 213
R (Wilkinson) v Broadmoor Special Hospital Authority [2002] 1 WLR 419

confidence.notes: Directions judgment only; substantive closure lawfulness not finally determined.

notes: Section 44 mandatory injunction for Russian bank authorisation documents; Hiscox followed.

enrichment.short_title: Cetelem v Roust Holdings: urgent section 44 order for CBR share-transfer documents
key_facts: Cetelem agreed to buy a 50% stake in Roust Cetelem Ltd from Roust Holdings for about US$320 million under an English-law ICC arbitration agreement.
Central Bank of Russia authorisation was a condition precedent expiring on 31 January 2005; extensive documentation had to be submitted by late December 2004.
After a 22 December letter alleging destroyed trust, Cetelem obtained without-notice freezing relief and sought a mandatory order compelling document production.
Beatson J granted mandatory relief under section 44 requiring RHL to take reasonable lawful measures to deliver listed documents by noon on 30 December.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent return date on without-notice freezing and mandatory injunction applications in support of imminent London arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Mandatory injunction granted in narrowed terms mirroring clause 6.8 obligations; freezing order continued; permission to appeal refused; privacy application refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 44(3) permits urgent pre-arbitration orders for a proposed party where necessary to preserve assets or support the arbitral process; a mandatory order requiring contractual cooperation to submit regulatory documents does not finally determine merits and may be enforced where the respondent can control group companies.
legal_issues: Whether section 44(3) applies before arbitral proceedings are commenced
Whether mandatory injunction relief was too uncertain under Redland Bricks v Morris
Whether the court lacked jurisdiction over BVI defendant with assets abroad
Whether freezing order should continue pending arbitration
linked_authorities: Hiscox Underwriting Ltd v Dickson [2004] EWHC 479
Motorola Credit Corporation v Uzan (No 2) [2003] EWCA Civ 752
Redland Bricks Ltd v Morris [1970] AC 652

notes: Coroner post-mortem permission appeal refused; limited examination may suffice.

enrichment.short_title: Kasperowicz v Plymouth coroner: post-mortem after uncertified death of elderly grandmother
key_facts: Adela Kasperowicz, 88, died on 30 December 2004 after respiratory difficulties at home following recent hospital treatment for pneumonia and sepsis.
No attending doctor would certify the medical cause of death; the coroner treated it as a sudden death of unknown cause requiring investigation.
The family, citing Catholic beliefs that the body should remain intact, sought to restrain post-mortem examination and preferred MRI scanning.
Gray J refused injunctive relief; the Court of Appeal renewed application was dismissed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against refusal of injunction restraining coroner-directed post-mortem examination.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; coroner lawfully entitled to order section 19 post-mortem where no practitioner certificate exists; family concerns are humanitarian not legal grounds to halt the process.
enrichment.ratio: Where no attending medical practitioner certifies cause of death, independent ascertainment through coroner investigation is required by law; the coroner may limit examination appropriately but need not abandon post-mortem merely because the family knows a probable cause.
legal_issues: Whether death was 'sudden' within section 8(1)(b) when respiratory failure followed prior illness
Whether family knowledge of pneumonia/sepsis obviated need for post-mortem
Whether MRI scanning could replace invasive autopsy as a matter of law
Whether coroner decision was irrational or unlawful
